newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: SE Asian trio arrive in Cambodia for crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian trio arrive in Cambodia for crisis talks.

text.p: Envoys from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) arrived in Phnom Penh on Saturday for talks with powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who earlier rejected foreign interference in Cambodia's affairs.

The envoys, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, Prachuab Chaiyasarn of Thailand and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines, declined to answer reporters' questions when they arrived at Phnom Penh's airport.
The three envoys met King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing on Thursday and had talks with ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, in Bangkok on Friday.

Hun Sen, who removed Ranariddh in a bloody power-grab on July 6, on Friday dismissed international efforts to solve his country's political crisis and told foreigners, including ASEAN, to stay out of the country's affairs.
He said he would meet the three ASEAN envoys in Phnom Penh on Saturday, but appeared irritated with their diplomatic efforts.
Cambodia, he said, could survive without ASEAN.

"I will sit down and listen to them," he said, but added: "No foreigner can control Hun Sen. I will ask them to finish the problem tomorrow so they won't have to bother about Cambodia any more... Please don't interfere.
"If they don't let us join ASEAN, we won't join. If we don't join ASEAN, it won't be the death of us," he said.
ASEAN postponed Cambodia's entry to the grouping indefinitely in response to Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.

But Alatas said in Bangkok it was wrong to say ASEAN was interfering in Cambodia's affairs because it was consulting all parties to the conflict. "ASEAN cannot be accused of departing from its hallowed principle of non-interference," he said.
Ranariddh told reporters after three hours of talks with the ASEAN trio he wanted to avoid a new civil war in Cambodia.

"A new civil war in Cambodia would mean more destruction and more suffering for my already unfortunate Cambodia. I really agree with what ASEAN has done and what it is going to do in the days if not weeks to come."
Ung Huot, nominated to become Cambodia's First Prime Minister, has asked ASEAN to admit the strife-torn nation to the regional grouping at its annual foreign ministers' meeting.

Ung Huot, in letters to the seven ASEAN foreign ministers, copies of which were released by his ministry on Friday, said Cambodia was now politically stable and should be admitted to ASEAN at their meeting in Kuala Lumpur on July 23 as earlier planned.

"I firmly hope to meet your kind consideration to admit the Kingdom of Cambodia as a member of ASEAN on 23 July, 1997, as (had) been decided at the Special Meeting of ASEAN foreign ministers on 31 May 1997," the letter said.

Ung Huot, who is also foreign minister, told his counterparts that members of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party and Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party agreed to nominate him first prime minister, replacing the ousted prince.
The nomination was approved by Hun Sen's party but the United States has refused to recognise it, saying there was not evidence that Ung Huot's selection was made on a free and fair basis.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Burma and Laos will become full members next week.
